stimulus:
For some years I continued averse from mentioning this event, deeming it so horrible that I shrank from recording it . . . For even Antichrist will spare such as follow him, but these Tatars [a common synonym for the Mongols] spared none, slaying women and men and children, ripping open pregnant women and killing unborn babes.

They need no commissariat, nor the conveyance of supplies, for they have with them sheep, cows, and horses, the flesh of which they eat, naught else. And so, when they alight anywhere, they have need of nothing from without. As for their religion, they worship the sun when it rises, and regard nothing as unlawful, for they eat all beasts, even dogs, pigs, and the like; nor do they recognise the marriage-tie, for several men are in marital relations with one woman, and if a child is born, it knows not who its father is.

Therefore, Islam and the Muslims have been afflicted during this period with calamities wherewith no people hath been visited. These Tatars (may God confound them!) came from the East, and wrought deeds which horrify all who hear of them, and which you shall, please God, see set forth in full detail in their proper connection.

—Ibn al-Athir, Arab historian, 
On the Tatars
 (ca. 1220)
stem: The above author is reacting to which major historical development?
options: (A) The victory of Mamluk cavalry over Mongol armies at Ain Jalut
(B) The westward expansion of Genghis Khan’s Mongol Empire
(C) The Mongol conquest of Byzantium
(D) The establishment of Kublai Khan’s Mongol dynasty in China
explanation: The Mongols, also known as Tatars, emerged from present-day Mongolia and, under the leadership of Genghis Khan, conquered much of China and Central Asia between 1206 and 1227. They gained even more territory in the years that followed. This passage describes the Mongols’ clash with the Islamic world, making (C) and (D) unsuitable. (Also, the Mongols never took Byzantium, and Kublai Khan reigned years after this text was written.) The author’s gloomy tone does not seem to describe the kind of triumph described in (A) (which also happened some time after the text was written).

stem: Which of the following characterizes the author’s view of the Mongols?
options: (A) He depicts them as civilized adversaries, equal to his own people in social and cultural advancement.
(B) He regards them as divine retribution, sent as a punishment for the sins of all Muslims.
(C) He sees their invasion dispassionately, as part of the natural flow of human events.
(D) He writes of them as violent barbarians of unprecedented ferocity.
explanation: The author clearly views the Mongols negatively, rendering (A) and (C) erroneous. While it was common to refer to invaders like the Mongols and the Huns as “scourges of God,” and while the author indeed describes the Mongols’ arrival as an “affliction” to Muslims, he does not go so far as to connect it with Allah’s will, so (B) is not correct either. Instead, the author heavily emphasizes everything that was violent and primitive about the Mongols, leaving (D) as the only correct response.

stem: Which of the following items associated with the Mongols seems LEAST compatible with the impression of them given by the author?
options: (A) The forced recruitment of soldiers and skilled artisans from conquered peoples
(B) The organization of a hardy and mobile cavalry army
(C) The enforcement of law and order to safeguard commerce along the Silk Road
(D) The massacre of civilians after the taking of cities that refused to surrender immediately
explanation: The Mongols did all of these things as they acquired new territory and imposed their rule. Not surprisingly, traditional accounts of the Mongols tend to emphasize the undeniably violent aspects of their empire building, and the author certainly follows in this vein. Running against this stereotype, however, some Mongol practices were more constructive and stabilizing, and these have received more attention in recent years. Answer (C) is the only response that falls into this category.

stem: What long-term regional consequence did the development described by the author have for the Middle East?
options: (A) The destruction of the Abbasid Caliphate
(B) The adoption by all Mongols of Arabic as the written script for their language
(C) The long-term persecution of Islam in Mongol-held territory
(D) The permanent displacement of Persians from their homeland to the Mediterranean coast
explanation: This question requires some knowledge of the topic’s wider context. The outcomes described in (B) and (D) never happened, and because the Mongols often adopted cultural and religious practices from the people they conquered, the opposite of (C) actually took place, as many Mongols in fact converted to Islam. The most striking political impact of the Mongol invasions on the Middle East was the killing of the last Abbasid caliph upon the fall of Baghdad in 1258, as described in (A).

stimulus: Map depicting Bantu languages (in dark gray) as part of the Niger-Congo language family (Wikipedia Commons)
stem: The prevalence of Bantu languages in sub-Saharan Africa between 1200 and 1450 is best explained by
options: (A) the influence of Islam, brought from the desert by Berber nomads.
(B) the long migration of Bantu peoples throughout most of this region.
(C) short, decisive wars of conquest from the north to the south.
(D) participation in the Indian Ocean trade network.
explanation: The foundational factor in shaping the human history of sub-Saharan Africa is the migration of the Bantu-speaking peoples, a process that unfolded over centuries. Answer (D) describes another important trend but a later and less fundamental one. Answer (A) is more relevant to West Africa, and (C) is both generic and, in characterizing the spread of languages as a short-term trend, erroneous.

stimulus: Map depicting Bantu languages (in dark gray) as part of the Niger-Congo language family (Wikipedia Commons)
stem: Which of the following facts about sub-Saharan Africa between 1200 and 1450 might this map do the most to potentially obscure?
options: (A) Although limited in size, European settlements on sub-Saharan coastlines came to have a disproportionately large impact on Africa as a whole.
(B) An exceptionally high degree of cultural and linguistic diversity prevailed in the sub-Saharan parts of Africa.
(C) Geographical isolation tended to cut off much of sub-Saharan Africa from trade networks that extended beyond the continent.
(D) Islam spread to more parts of sub-Saharan Africa than is commonly thought.
explanation: Answer (C) is not true at all, and the issues touched on in (A) and (D) have little to do with the subject of the map, making it difficult for the map to create misleading impressions about them. What is true is the fact that, despite the common origin of Bantu languages, their evolution over time has caused them to diverge considerably—just as languages do in all large linguistic groups, such as English and Russian within the Indo-European family. Various Bantu languages are mutually incomprehensible, whereas the map in question might give the impression that they are more alike than they really are.

stem: What non-African language would have had the largest influence over Africa’s eastern coast between 1200 and 1450?
options: (A) Persian
(B) Hindi
(C) Arabic
(D) Turkish
explanation: Answers (A) and (D) describe languages too far away to have had the sort of impact referred to in the question. Because of the Indian Ocean trade network, (B) would not be an unreasonable guess, but the influence of Arabic culture and language all along the East African coast was both deep and long-lasting. Languages such as Swahili bear the clear marks of that influence. Answer (C) is by far the best choice.

stimulus:
Christine asks Reason why women aren’t allowed in courts of law, and Reason’s reply.

Christine: “Most honourable and worthy lady, your excellent arguments have satisfied my curiosity in so many areas. Yet, if you don’t mind, I’d like you to explain to me why women are allowed neither to present a case at a trial, nor bear witness, nor pass sentence since some men have claimed that it’s all because of some woman or other who behaved badly in a court of law.”

Reason: “My dear daughter, that whole ridiculous story is a malicious fabrication. But to come back to your question, you might as well ask why God didn’t command men to perform women’s tasks and women those of men. One could say that just as a wise and prudent lord organizes his household into different domains and operates a strict division of labour amongst his workforce, so God created man and woman to serve Him in different ways and to help and comfort one another, according to a similar division of labour. To this end, He endowed each sex with the qualities and attributes which they need to perform the tasks for which they are cut out. God gave men strong, powerful bodies to stride about and to speak boldly, which explains why it is men who learn the law and maintain the rule of justice. In those instances where someone refuses to uphold the law which has been established by right, men must enforce it through the use of arms and physical strength, which women clearly could not do. Even though God has often endowed many women with great intelligence, it would not be right for them to abandon their customary modesty and to go about bringing cases before a court, as there are already enough men to do so. However, if there are those who maintain that women aren’t 
intelligent
 enough to learn the law, I would contradict them by citing numerous examples of women of both the past and the present who were great philosophers and who excelled in many disciplines which are much more difficult than simply learning the laws and the statutes of men. I’ll tell you more about these women in a moment.”

—Christine de Pizan, French poet, allegorical conversation with the female embodiment of Reason, excerpted from 
The Book of the City of Ladies
, 1405
stem: The author’s main purpose in this passage is to
options: (A) advocate for complete gender equality.
(B) argue that many women are intellectually equal to men.
(C) plead for an equal role for women in the practice of law.
(D) justify traditional explanations for the supposed inferiority of women.
explanation: In this passage, the author goes farther than the stance described in (D) (which she clearly disagrees with) but does not go as far as that described in (C), or especially (A). As one of the first women to make a living as a professional writer (and arguably the first one to do so in Europe), Christine de Pizan most definitely rejected the notion that women were inherently less intelligent than men, but she did not believe that God or nature had designed men and women to play the same role in society or everyday life.

stem: Which of the following best seems to characterize the author’s view of the relationship between men and women?
options: (A) God designed men and women for different purposes, but their roles should be considered equally valuable.
(B) The Christian Bible has ordained that men should in all ways exercise authority over women.
(C) As a matter of biological fact, men are both physically and mentally stronger than women.
(D) The present state of male dominance over women is unjust and must be ended as soon as possible.
explanation: The author depicts herself as taking part in a dialogue with a female personification of Reason (which, considering the long-standing bias that associates rationality with male thinking, is a powerful statement in and of itself). Nonetheless, the author also signals the importance of Christian belief as part of her worldview. Answer (C) represents a more materialist way of looking at gender questions and is sexist in a way the author would not agree with. Answer (D) represents the polar opposite of (C) but is more modern and ethically abstract than the author’s outlook appears to be. Answer (B) uses Christian belief to justify gender inequality in the highly traditional and literal way that many men employed over centuries, but the author does not subscribe to this understanding of Christianity. Her reference to a “division of labor” best matches the point of view given in (A).

stem: How might the author’s views about women be most usefully assessed from the perspective of modern historians of gender?
options: (A) She was not committed enough to gender equality to be considered part of the feminist tradition.
(B) Her outlook conforms closely with modern understandings of feminism.
(C) Her writings harmfully reinforced the patriarchal notions of her time.
(D) Although influenced by certain assumptions from her era, she can be considered a forerunner of feminist thinking.
explanation: Not all of Christine de Pizan’s views on women seem bold by today’s standards, making (B) a poor choice, but this question is a good reminder of the perils of “presentism,” or measuring the past by the standards of one’s own time, a tendency one can see in (A) and (C). It would be hard to maintain that all of de Pizan’s views fit comfortably with modern understandings of gender equality, but they were certainly far ahead of the patriarchal attitudes that dominated in medieval and Renaissance Europe, making (D) the best answer.

stem: What system of labor would most likely have been used to organize this sort of agricultural work?
options: (A) Indentured servitude
(B) Sharecropping

(C) The 
mit’a
(D) Chattel slavery
explanation:
The 
mit’a
 system, employed by many Andean societies, including the Inca, was a form of corvée labor, in which a central political authority compels subjects to work for a certain amount of time, without wages, on a large public project or task. It does not involve actual ownership of people, as in (D), the repayment of debts, as in (A), or a rental arrangement, as in (B). Spanish colonizers adapted the 
mit’a
 system to their own purposes after conquering the Inca in the 1500s.
